Building a Desktop OS in the Browser: My Portfolio Site
I built my personal website as a simulated desktop operating system with draggable windows, a terminal, and 3D wallpapers. Here's how it works and what I learned along the way.

Most developer portfolios are straightforward: a hero section, some project cards, a contact form. Mine boots into a fake operating system.

When I started my CS degree at SNHU, I wanted a portfolio that reflected how I actually work: multiple windows open, a terminal always running, and a desktop environment I can tweak endlessly. So I built [wardbryan3.github.io](https://wardbryan3.github.io) as a browser-based OS simulation.

## The Core Idea

The site uses [Astro](https://astro.build) as the static site framework with React handling the interactive components. On desktop (769px+), visitors see a full desktop environment with draggable, resizable windows managed by a [Zustand](https://github.com/pmndrs/zustand) store. On mobile, it falls back to a simpler dashboard.

The window manager tracks six apps (so far) a file explorer for my projects, a terminal, a music player, a settings panel, a resume viewer, and a trash can. Each window stores its position, size, and z-index in the Zustand store, which is persisted to localStorage under `portfolio-os-settings`. This means if you close and reopen a window, it remembers where it was.

## The Terminal

The most fun part was the terminal. It opens automatically on boot and supports a handful of custom commands: `help`, `cd`, `ls`, `whoami`, `fastfetch`, `clear`, and a few easter eggs. Running `fastfetch` shows a fastfetch-style system info display with fields like name, status, tools, and project count. The terminal is a real React component that reads from the same data sources as the rest of the site — project and blog collections — so counts stay accurate. You can also use `grep` to search through the whole site by a single word. `find` Also works, and searches by titles.

## 3D Wallpapers

I wanted more visual interest than a static background, so I added three real-time wallpapers using Three.js via react-three-fiber: a particle field, a digital rain (Matrix-style), and a hex grid that responds to mouse movement. Users can switch between them in Settings. Each wallpaper is lazy-loaded, so you only pay for the one you're using.

## What I Learned

This project reinforced a few concepts from my coursework:

**State management at scale.** Managing multiple windows with position, focus, minimize, maximize, and z-index taught me why global state stores exist. My first attempt used React state and callbacks passed through props, it became unmanageable at about four windows. Zustand's `set`/`get` API with selectors made it trivial.

**Astro's island architecture.** Astro ships zero JavaScript by default and only hydrates interactive components marked with client directives. The desktop OS renders with `client:media="(min-width: 769px)"`, it never even loads on mobile. This keeps the bundle small and the Lighthouse score high.

**Content collections beat hardcoding.** Defining my projects and blog posts as typed MDX collections with Zod schemas means the data is validated, queryable, and reusable across pages and the terminal. Updating a project description in one MDX file propagates everywhere.

## A Setup That Helps

Working on a project like this with multiple windows open (editor, dev server, browser dev tools) made me appreciate screen real estate. After a semester of wrestling with window tabs on a laptop screen, I picked up a [Dell S2722QC 27-inch 4K Monitor](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B09TQJ7TSZ). Being able to keep reference docs on one screen and code on the other is probably the single biggest productivity boost I've found as a student developer.

If you're building something similar — or any substantial side project — I'd recommend giving yourself the desk space to see it all at once. Your future self will thank you when you're not alt-tabbing between eight windows.

The full source is on [GitHub](https://github.com/wardbryan3/wardbryan3.github.io) if you want to poke around or steal ideas for your own portfolio.

Testing Multiple Headings and Long Scrolling Content
A long test post with multiple heading levels for verifying TOC and layout behavior.

## Introduction

This is a test post designed to be long enough to require scrolling. It contains multiple headings at different levels so we can verify the table of contents, the scroll tracking, the prev/next navigation, and the overall layout.

The purpose of this post is purely functional testing. Each section below covers a different aspect of the site's behavior.

## Getting Started With Testing

Before we dive into the details, let's set up some expectations. This section covers the basics of what we're testing.

### Test Environment

The test environment consists of a mobile-responsive Astro site with a three-column blog layout. The layout includes:

- A left sidebar with blog navigation
- A center content area with the article text
- A right column with an auto-generated table of contents
- A terminal panel that can be expanded or collapsed

### Scope of Testing

We are verifying several features simultaneously:

- The table of contents should list all h2 and h3 headings
- Scrolling should highlight the active heading in the TOC
- The prev/next navigation should appear at the bottom
- The layout should be responsive at different breakpoints

## Detailed Analysis

Now let's go deeper into each component that needs verification. This section contains several subsections.

### Table of Contents Behavior

The TOC is built using a React component with IntersectionObserver. It watches all h2 and h3 elements in the article and highlights the one currently in view. This requires:

1. Correct heading IDs generated by Astro's MDX processor
2. The observer correctly ordering headings by DOM position
3. Proper cleanup of stale active states

### Terminal Persistence

The terminal uses sessionStorage to persist its open/closed state across page navigations. When you navigate from one blog post to another, the terminal should remember whether it was expanded or collapsed.

### Mobile Responsiveness

On viewports narrower than 768px, the layout collapses to a single column. The sidebar and TOC are hidden, and the terminal switches to a floating overlay mode. A toggle button in the nav bar opens and closes it.

## Code Examples

Here is a block of code to demonstrate syntax highlighting and scrolling:

```python
def fibonacci(n):
    """Generate the nth Fibonacci number."""
    if n <= 0:
        return 0
    elif n == 1:
        return 1
    else:
        a, b = 0, 1
        for _ in range(2, n + 1):
            a, b = b, a + b
        return b

def main():
    for i in range(20):
        print(f"fib({i}) = {fibonacci(i)}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Performance Considerations

This section discusses performance aspects of the layout.

### Render Performance

The page renders a React terminal component with `client:load`, which means it hydrates immediately. The TOC also uses a React component with `client:load`. These are the two interactive elements on the page.

### Network Performance

The page loads Google Fonts (Inter and JetBrains Mono) from an external CDN. The RSS feed link enables autodiscovery. The build output is a static site with prerendered HTML for each blog post.

## Edge Cases

Let's cover some edge cases that could break the layout.

### Very Long Headings That Might Wrap to Multiple Lines

This is a deliberately long heading that exists solely to test what happens when the table of contents entry wraps to multiple lines and whether the layout stays intact under such conditions without breaking or overflowing.

### No Headings

If a blog post has no h2 or h3 headings, the TOC column should simply not render. The layout should degrade gracefully to a two-column or single-column layout depending on the viewport.

### Single Heading

If a blog post has only one heading, the TOC should still render correctly with a single entry. The IntersectionObserver should track it properly.

## Conclusion

This test post covers all the major features of the blog layout. With sufficient length and multiple heading levels, it provides a reliable way to verify that the TOC, terminal, navigation, and responsive design all work correctly together.
